# ghax A minimalist, terminal-native agent written in Go that takes on a **shape** — a design partner, a spec implementer, a telemetry watcher — and runs as a well-behaved citizen of the [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) runtime. Disclaimer: This works for me -- that's the entire guarantee. Built with AI in the loop, so check your own biases before you love it or hate it on principle. Use at your own risk, fork freely, and don't @ me when it explodes. (But do drop me a note if it helps -- pay it forward.) > **Status: working, early.** The engine, three loop modes, provider adapters (local, OpenAI, > Anthropic, and an offline mock), the compiled-in tools, config/shapes, sessions, and the herdr > client are implemented and tested (`make test`). It has not yet been exercised against a wide > range of live models. See [VISION.md](./VISION.md) for the why and [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md) for > the how. > > Try it with no model backend at all: `make build && ./bin/ghax --provider mock -p "hello"`. --- ## The problem You end up wanting the same agent for very different jobs. One moment it should be a thinking partner reasoning through a design with a big model. The next it should grind a project to a written spec, unattended. Sometimes it shouldn't be coding at all — it should sit on a telemetry stream and react when something interesting happens. Those jobs want different prompts, tools, models, and rhythms, but the machine underneath them is the same: read input, build context, ask a model, run tools, loop. Most agents make you pick one job and one runtime. And when you run several at once — across a laptop, a build server, and an edge box — you lose track of which one is working, which is stuck, and which is done. ghax is one small binary that solves both. You give it a **shape** (config, not code) and it becomes the agent that job needs. And because it reports its real state to herdr, a fleet of shaped instances stays legible: herdr never has to guess what any ghax is doing. ## Why build this? Because the agent should run on **your** inference, not someone else's API. The premise: you run one or more inference servers — Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, TGI — on a workstation, a GPU box, a DGX, or a small cluster, and you front them with [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/), which exposes a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint with model routing, fallback, aliases, key management, and usage accounting. ghax points at that one endpoint. That buys you: - **Traffic stays on your network by default.** ghax only ever talks to your LiteLLM endpoint. Nothing leaves your network unless *you* wire an external backend into LiteLLM — and that is a single, deliberate config change in one file, not a decision scattered across every agent. - **One place for config, keys, routing, and monitoring.** Point a whole fleet of ghax agents at a single LiteLLM: model choices, provider keys, routing and fallback, budgets, rate limits, and usage logging all live there. You configure and observe every agent from one control point. - **No per-token cost and no rate limits** you did not set yourself — for anything served locally. - **The same agent everywhere.** One static Go binary, from an edge SBC to a Kubernetes pod, all talking to the same gateway. Most agents assume a hosted cloud API, a heavyweight runtime, or a plugin marketplace. ghax assumes you own the inference and want a small, inspectable, scriptable tool that takes on whatever shape the job needs — and stays legible when you run a fleet of them under herdr. It descends from [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax) and keeps its restraint; [VISION.md](./VISION.md) records the full rationale and the deliberate omissions. ## Why this and not hax, pi, or OMP? These are the neighbors. Short version: **ghax is hax's philosophy in Go, with a first-class observe mode and herdr citizenship, built to point at your own LiteLLM-fronted inference.** **vs [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax)** — hax is the direct ancestor, and ghax keeps almost all of it: one small binary, local-first, inspectable, no plugins / MCP / permission prompts, presets. What ghax changes: - **Go, not C.** One statically cross-compiled binary for the whole spectrum — edge SBC → server → Kubernetes pod — with goroutines and `context` instead of hand-rolled threads. Same footprint discipline, less ceremony. - **A first-class observe loop.** hax is request/response only; it can't sit on a telemetry stream and react. ghax's `observe` mode (sources → triggers → bounded reactions) is a peer of the REPL. - **herdr-native.** ghax ships authoritative status hooks, a screen manifest, and shape/model metadata so a fleet is legible; hax is just a well-behaved Unix tool. - **Shapes select the loop mode**, not only the prompt/model — so one binary is a REPL, a script step, or a watcher. If you only want coding at the terminal, in C, with no watcher and no fleet, use hax — it's the smaller, more proven thing. ghax is for when you also want the observe mode, herdr fleet visibility, and Go's one-binary reach across your hardware. **vs pi and OMP (oh-my-pi)** — these are richer, batteries-included agents with **package ecosystems** ([pi.dev](https://pi.dev/) packages) and full TUIs, and they're first-class herdr citizens too. ghax goes the other way on purpose: - **No package runtime, plugin ABI, or marketplace.** Extension is config, `SKILL.md`, and external CLIs — the hax stance. Less power, far less surface to audit, version, or break. - **One small static binary, not a platform.** Nothing to install beyond the binary; nothing dynamic to load at runtime. - **Shaped for non-coding jobs too.** The same engine watches telemetry or processes a stream, not only writes code. - **Citizen, not conductor.** ghax reports state to herdr but does not orchestrate peers or host a plugin surface — orchestration stays outside the process. If you want the ecosystem — installable packages, a plugin surface, a full-screen TUI — reach for pi or OMP. ghax is for when you want the *smallest* thing that can be many shapes, runs on your own inference, and stays legible in a fleet. The common thread: **you own the inference (LiteLLM in front of your servers), you want one auditable binary, and you want it to become whatever shape the job needs.** ## What it is - **One static Go binary.** Cross-compiles for servers, SBCs, and edge devices. Small footprint — it leaves the RAM for your models. - **Your inference, via LiteLLM.** Point ghax at a LiteLLM proxy fronting your inference server(s) (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp). One OpenAI-compatible endpoint, many models; `type: local` auto-discovers the served model. Cloud APIs work too, but self-hosted is the assumption. See [Model backend](#model-backend-litellm-in-front-of-your-inference). - **Three loop modes.** `interactive` (a REPL), `oneshot` (`-p`, clean stdout, resumable — the Unix seam for scripts), and `observe` (a long-running, event-driven watcher). - **A herdr citizen.** Reports authoritative status (`working`/`idle`/`done`) and rich metadata over the herdr socket, ships a screen manifest as a fallback, and resumes cleanly. It does not orchestrate other agents — that stays outside the process. - **Minimalist and inspectable, on purpose.** No MCP, no plugin ABI, no marketplace, no per-command permission prompts. Extend it with external CLIs, skills, and config. See [VISION.md](./VISION.md#9-non-goals) for what it deliberately omits and why. ## Model backend: LiteLLM in front of your inference ghax speaks the OpenAI-compatible chat API and is designed to point at a **LiteLLM proxy** that fronts one or more inference servers. Run a whole fleet of ghax agents against a single LiteLLM: ```mermaid flowchart LR g1["ghax · design-partner"] --> lite g2["ghax · spec-implementer"] --> lite g3["ghax · telemetry-watcher"] --> lite lite["LiteLLM proxy
models · keys · routing · budgets · usage"] lite --> ollama["Ollama"] lite --> vllm["vLLM / TGI / llama.cpp"] lite -. you configure this .-> cloud["cloud API
(Anthropic, Ollama Cloud, …)"] ``` LiteLLM is your **single control point**: it is the one place to add models, hold provider keys, set routing and budgets, and watch usage across every agent. **Traffic never leaves your network unless you add an external backend there** — a deliberate, auditable change in one file, not something any individual ghax decides. Point ten agents at one LiteLLM and you configure and monitor all ten from that one place. Configure a provider pointed at your LiteLLM endpoint. `type: local` auto-discovers the served model from `/v1/models`, so the common case is just a base URL: ```json { "default_provider": "dgx", "providers": { "dgx": { "type": "local", "base_url": "http://dgx:4000/v1", "model": "local-qwen", "params": { "temperature": 0.7, "top_p": 0.8, "top_k": 20, "repetition_penalty": 1.05 } } } } ``` `params` are passed through verbatim, so backend-specific sampling controls (Ollama's `top_k`, `repetition_penalty`) reach the model through LiteLLM. Per-response token usage flows back too, so `/usage` works on local models. ghax is not *locked* to LiteLLM — because it is an OpenAI-compatible client you can point it straight at Ollama, llama.cpp, or a cloud API (`openai` / `anthropic` provider types). But the assumed deployment, and the one the defaults and docs are written for, is LiteLLM fronting your own inference. ### How LiteLLM routes by model name ghax always sends the request to the **one** LiteLLM endpoint; the `model` name in the request is the routing key. ghax's own `provider` (`dgx`) only means *"talk to LiteLLM"* — it is **not** the upstream provider. LiteLLM looks the model name up in its `model_list` and the matching entry decides the backend: ```yaml # litellm config.yaml — the routing table model_list: - model_name: local-qwen # the alias ghax asks for litellm_params: model: ollama_chat/qwen3-coder-next # provider prefix "ollama_chat" -> Ollama api_base: http://localhost:11434 - model_name: claude # alias litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 # provider prefix "anthropic" -> Anthropic api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY # the key lives HERE, not in ghax ``` The backend is chosen from the **provider prefix** on `litellm_params.model` (the part before the `/`): `anthropic/…`, `openai/…`, `ollama/…`, `gemini/…`, `bedrock/…`, `azure/…`, or `openai/…` with a custom `api_base` for any OpenAI-compatible server. `api_base` says where, `api_key` says with what. The flow: ghax `POST /v1/chat/completions {"model":"claude", …}` → LiteLLM matches `claude` in the `model_list` → translates the OpenAI request into that backend's native API → calls it (with the key LiteLLM holds) → translates the response back to OpenAI shape for ghax. ghax sent only `"model": "claude"` and never knew Anthropic was behind it. So picking a model in ghax (`--model claude`, or a shape's `model`) is just choosing a `model_name` LiteLLM knows. Two things LiteLLM adds at this layer, invisibly to ghax: several `model_list` entries sharing one `model_name` get **load-balanced / failed over**, and you can declare `fallbacks` (e.g. `claude → local-qwen` on error). ## Prerequisites - Go (recent stable) to build the binary. - A model endpoint: a **LiteLLM proxy fronting your inference server(s)** (the assumed setup), or directly an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoint. The offline `mock` provider needs nothing. - Optional: [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) if you want fleet visibility and persistent sessions. ## Quick start ```sh # Build the single binary. make build # -> ./bin/ghax # No model needed — the offline mock provider echoes, to prove the loop works. ./bin/ghax --provider mock -p "hello ghax" # Interactive, against your configured LiteLLM endpoint (model auto-discovered). ghax # One prompt, clean stdout — the scripting seam. ghax -p "list the TODOs in this repo" printf "explain main.go" | ghax -p # Run under a named shape. ghax --shape design-partner ghax --shape spec-implementer -p "implement the spec in docs/DESIGN.md" # An observe agent watching a stream and reacting. tail -F /var/log/telemetry.jsonl | ghax --shape telemetry-watcher # Continue or resume a session. ghax -c # continue the latest session for this directory ghax --resume # pick a past session ``` ## Configuration Configuration is plain text under the XDG config directory. Every setting has a canonical key and, where it makes sense, an environment variable. Resolution order, most explicit wins: **CLI flag > environment variable > saved runtime selection > config file default.** A **shape** is a named config bundle — loop mode, provider, model, effort, system prompt, tool profile, `skills` (`SKILL.md` directories composed into the system prompt), and (for observe shapes) sources and triggers. Shapes are files you keep in a repo. `effort` maps to the backend's reasoning control (`reasoning_effort` / extended `thinking`) for reasoning-capable models. A top-level `compact_at` token estimate enables automatic history compaction (default 12000; `0` disables; the `/compact` command works regardless). A shape's `system` prompt may be inline text or loaded from a file with the `FILE:` prefix (`"system": "FILE: ./prompts/coder.md"`); a named file that is missing is an error. See [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md#7-configuration-and-shapes) for the format and the full setting reference. **Project instructions.** ghax automatically loads the `AGENTS.md` hierarchy: on each run it walks up from the working directory (stopping at the repo root / home), collecting every `AGENTS.md` and appending them to the system prompt, nearest-wins. Disable with `"auto_instructions": false`. ### Example shapes Ready-to-copy configs live in [`examples/`](./examples/) — run one with `GHAX_CONFIG=examples/ ./bin/ghax` (from the repo root; see [examples/README.md](./examples/README.md)): | Config | Shape(s) | Demonstrates | | --- | --- | --- | | [`coding-agent.json`](./examples/coding-agent.json) | `coder` | The basic one — an interactive coding agent, full tool set, `system` prompt from a file (`FILE:`). | | [`design-partner.json`](./examples/design-partner.json) | `design-partner`, `coder` | Use a paid cloud model only for the thinking-heavy role: `design-partner` asks LiteLLM for the `claude` model (`effort: high`, read-only) while `coder` stays on the free local model — no API key in ghax; the key lives in LiteLLM. | | [`telemetry-watcher.json`](./examples/telemetry-watcher.json) | `watcher` | An `observe` shape that watches stdin and reacts only to lines matching `error/fail/critical/panic`. | | [`reviewer-with-skill.json`](./examples/reviewer-with-skill.json) | `reviewer` | A one-shot reviewer that loads a `SKILL.md` (a Go review checklist) into its system prompt. | A shape is just a block in the config: ```json "shapes": { "coder": { "loop": "interactive", "system": "FILE: examples/prompts/coder.md", "tools": ["read", "write", "edit", "bash", "task"] } } ``` **Interactive UI.** On a terminal, `ghax` clears the screen and renders a styled REPL: a header box (model · provider · shape · status), a boxed prompt, streamed responses, and a keybinding footer. Type `/help` for commands — `/clear` (fresh conversation), `/compact` (summarize history), `/usage` (session token totals), `/copy` (last response to clipboard), `/session`. `Ctrl-C` interrupts the current turn (not the program); `Ctrl-D` exits. When output is piped it falls back to a plain prompt so scripts are unaffected. `NO_COLOR` disables styling; `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1` forces it (e.g. piping into `less -R`). ## Common tasks | Task | How | | --- | --- | | Choose the model/provider | Config `default_provider`/`model`, or the `--provider` / `--model` flags. | | REPL commands | `/help` lists them: `/clear`, `/compact`, `/usage`, `/copy`, `/session`. | | Run a shape unattended, bounded | `ghax --shape -p ""` with `max_turns` set in the shape. | | Watch a stream and react | An `observe` shape with a source and a trigger; pipe or configure the source. | | Drive a loop from a script | Wrap `ghax -p` / `ghax -c -p` in a shell loop (the composition seam). | | Inspect what was sent/received | The transcript and trace outputs; sessions are plain files. | | Run in a fleet | Launch shaped instances under herdr; status and metadata report automatically. | ## Project structure See [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md#3-package-layout) for the authoritative layout. ``` ghax/ cmd/ghax/ entrypoint + flag dispatch internal/agent/ core loop, item log, turn state machine (pure) internal/provider/ provider adapters: local, openai, anthropic, mock, sse internal/tool/ compiled-in tools: read, write, edit, bash, task internal/observe/ observe loop: sources, triggers, reactions internal/herdr/ herdr socket client + status reporting + manifest internal/config/ config + shape resolution internal/session/ resumable session persistence internal/terminal/ styled-output helpers (color, boxes, screen control) internal/app/ wiring + the three drivers internal/cli/ flag parsing internal/skill/ SKILL.md loading into the system prompt examples/ ready-to-copy config examples + prompt files + a sample skill VISION.md DESIGN.md README.md ``` ## herdr integration ghax is built to be the best-behaved citizen on the herdr runtime: authoritative state reporting, correct semantics for the observe loop (a quietly-watching agent reads as `idle`, not a hung `working` pane), rich shape/model metadata, and clean session resume. It consumes herdr; it does not orchestrate peers through the socket. Details in [VISION.md](./VISION.md#7-herdr-integration-the-best-behaved-citizen-on-the-runtime) and [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md#8-herdr-client). ## Documentation - [VISION.md](./VISION.md) — what ghax is for and the principles that constrain it. - [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md) — the architecture, packages, interfaces, and testing strategy. ## License MIT. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

# ghax

**A minimalist, terminal-native, shape-shifting agent written in Go — a first-class citizen of the [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) runtime.**

Vision document. Date-stamped 2026-09-12. This is a north star, not a spec. It describes what
ghax is for, the principles that constrain it, and the architecture those principles imply. It
does not commit to APIs or timelines.

---

## 1. The thesis

One agent binary. Many jobs. The job changes; the machine underneath does not.

An agent instance might be a **thinking partner** reasoning through a design with a foundation
model. Another might be a **spec implementer** grinding a project to a written specification.
Another might not be coding at all — it might sit on a **telemetry stream**, watching for
something interesting and reacting ad hoc. Each of those looks different from the outside. Each
wants a different system prompt, a different tool set, a different model, a different rhythm.

But the thing running underneath is the same: read input, build context, ask a model, dispatch
tools, loop. The **shape** differs; the fundamental capabilities do not.

ghax is that underlying thing — small, inspectable, one static binary — plus a disciplined way to
give it a shape. It descends directly from [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax), a
minimalist C coding agent, and it inherits hax's restraint on purpose. It adds three things hax
does not have, because our world needs them:

1. **Go.** Real concurrency, one cross-compiled binary, and a language that runs everywhere we
   deploy — from an Orange Pi at the edge to a Kubernetes pod.
2. **A first-class observe loop.** Not every useful agent is request/response. Some watch.
3. **Deep herdr citizenship.** When many shaped instances run at once, the runtime that herds
   them needs to know exactly what each one is doing, without guessing.

---

## 2. Lineage: what we keep from hax, what we change

hax earned its shape by saying no. We keep almost all of it and change three things.

### Kept

| hax principle | Why it survives in ghax |
| --- | --- |
| One binary, tiny footprint | An edge node has little RAM; leave it for the model. Go gives us the single binary; we defend the footprint. |
| Local models are first-class | Start a local server, point ghax at it, it discovers the model. Cloud is a config change, not a different product. |
| Respect the terminal | Stream Markdown and live tool output, preserve scrollback, never seize the terminal. |
| Inspectable | You can always see exactly what was sent to the model and what came back. Sessions and traces are plain files. |
| Extensibility from substrates already present | Config, Markdown files, and subprocesses — not a plugin ABI, not a marketplace. |
| Composes as a Unix tool | One-shot mode with clean stdout is the seam. Orchestration lives *outside* the process, where it can be versioned and tested. |
| No permission prompts | An in-process approval gate is not a security boundary. Isolation comes from the OS (container/VM). Restraint comes from the prompt and from bounded runs. |

### Changed

1. **C → Go.** hax hand-rolls threads, cleanup labels, and a JSON parser to stay lean. Go gives
   us goroutines, channels, `context.Cancellation`, and a standard library for free, and still
   compiles to one static binary. The footprint discipline stays; the ceremony goes.

2. **Request/response only → request/response *and* observe.** hax is a REPL: a turn is a
   round-trip. ghax keeps that and adds a peer: a long-running, event-driven loop that reacts to
   a stream. Same engine underneath (see §4).

3. **Runtime-agnostic → herdr-native.** hax is a well-behaved Unix tool and stops there. ghax is
   also a well-behaved Unix tool, but it additionally ships the hooks and the manifest that make
   it a *model-authoritative* citizen of herdr, so a fleet of shaped instances is legible at a
   glance (see §7).

### "Like pi, but in Go" — resolved

pi is small, ships first-class local models, and can be pointed at many jobs. That is the part we
want. We do **not** want pi's package/plugin runtime. ghax's answer to "add a capability" stays
pure hax: a CLI with a README, a skill that tells the model when to reach for it, or a
config-defined provider. See §6 and §9.

---

## 3. The core idea: one engine, many shapes

A **shape** is a named, versioned bundle that configures the engine for a job. It is a
config artifact, not code. A shape names:

- a **loop mode** — `interactive`, `oneshot`, or `observe`;
- a **provider + model + effort** — local or cloud, small or large;
- a **system prompt** — base and append, inline or from a file;
- a **tool profile** — which of the compiled-in tools are enabled, plus any external tools;
- optional **skills** and **project instructions** to load;
- optional **observe sources and triggers** (observe mode only).

Shapes are the same mechanism hax calls *presets*, widened to also select the loop mode and
observe wiring. Because a shape is just config, it is versionable, diffable, and shareable, and
it can live in a repo next to the code it works on.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Engine["ghax engine (one binary)"]
        core["agent core:\ncontext → model → tools → loop"]
    end
    A["shape: design-partner\ninteractive · big cloud model\nreasoning tools, no write"] --> core
    B["shape: spec-implementer\noneshot · coding model\nfull tool set, spec loaded"] --> core
    C["shape: telemetry-watcher\nobserve · small local model\nstream source + triggers"] --> core

# 5 Clever Names for ghax

## 1. **SHAPE** (Shape-Handling Agent for Persistent Execution)
- **Why it works:** Directly references the core concept—agents that take on different *shapes* for different jobs
- **Evokes:** Shape-shifting robotics, modular design, adaptable form
- **Tech appeal:** Clean, memorable, pronounceable, all-caps tech acronym style
- **Scalability:** SHAPE engine, SHAPE runtime, SHAPE CLI (shape)

## 2. **FORM** (Flexible Orchestrated Reasoning Machine)
- **Why it works:** "Form" is the philosophical opposite of "shape"—same concept, different framing; also suggests formation, transformation
- **Evokes:** Biological morphogenesis, robotics form factors, fluid adaptation
- **Tech appeal:** Short, powerful, works in plural (FORMs for fleets)
- **Bonus:** FORM and SHAPE pair beautifully: "shape your FORM" / "form your SHAPE"

## 3. **CHORUS** (Cooperative Homogeneous Orchestrated Utility System for Heterogeneous Tasks)
- **Why it works:** References the herdr runtime (a chorus of agents being conducted), and the idea that multiple shaped instances work together
- **Evokes:** Choral music (many voices, one harmony), swarm robotics, distributed coordination
- **Tech appeal:** Memorable, has musical/organizational metaphor, implies harmony

## 4. **POLYP** (Polymorphic Orchestrated Learning Agent)
- **Why it works:** Polyp = organism that can take many forms (like a jellyfish polyp); biological shape-shifting
- **Evokes:** Nature's master adapters, colonial intelligence, emergent behavior
- **Tech appeal:** Unexpected but precise, short, memorable, biological robotics vibe

## 5. **CHRYsalis** (Cognitive Homogeneous Runtime Yielding Adaptive Shape-shifting Intelligent Agent in a Liminal State)
- **Why it works:** Chrysalis is the pupal stage where an organism transforms—perfect metaphor for an agent that takes on different shapes
- **Evokes:** Metamorphosis, emerging robotics, becoming more than the sum of parts
- **Tech appeal:** Elegant, hints at transformation, works as Chrysalis (full) or Chrysal (abbreviated)

## Recommended: **SHAPE** or **FORM**

- **SHAPE** is the most direct reference to your core concept and easiest to explain
- **FORM** is the subtle reframe that feels more organic and robotic

Both maintain the "shape" metaphor while evolving beyond "ghax" to something that feels mature and aligned with emerging robotics.

Directly references your core concept—agents that take on different *shapes* for different jobs. Evokes shape-shifting robotics and modular adaptation.

A philosophical reframe: "form" vs "shape." Evokes biological morphogenesis, robotics form factors, and fluid adaptation.

References the herdr runtime and multiple shaped instances working together. Evokes choral harmony and swarm robotics.

## 4. **POLYP** (Polymorphic Orchestrated Learning Agent)
Polyps in nature can take many forms—perfect metaphor for shape-shifting agents. Short, biological, memorable.

## 5. **CHRYsalis** (Cognitive Homogeneous Runtime Yielding Adaptive Shape-shifting Intelligent Agent in a Liminal State)
The pupal stage where transformation happens—perfect metaphor for an agent that morphs into different roles.
